name: Brownish Vinaceous
lede: Brownish Vinaceous is a dusty pink-brown from Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature, built on *vinaceous*, Latin for wine-colored, with *brownish* pulling it away from true wine toward clay.

sections.title: Wine-colored, pulled toward brown
sections.body:
Ridgway's *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* (1912) lists Brownish Vinaceous on plate XXXIX, hue 5′′′, tone b [1]. Ridgway used *vinaceous*, from the Latin for wine, as a base family for a whole run of pink-browns; *brownish* is one of the modifiers he used to walk a hue away from that base toward a neighboring family [1]. The ISCC-NBS system placed it in its 1955 block 18, *light grayish red* [1].

The library's measurements place its nearest named neighbor as [[rosy-brown|Rosy Brown]], about 3 units off (tied with a couple of other dictionary names at nearly the same distance), and it sits about 8.8 units from the everyday name [[puce|Puce]], a darker, more purplish brown-pink [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color match to this swatch in 129 of 23,781 paintings, 0.54 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 57, more common than 52 percent of the named colors we track [3]. The sample is too thin for a reliable single-painter figure, so none is claimed here [3].

The color peaks in the 1900s, 1.9 times the expected rate across 1,674 paintings from that decade, and inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, sitting low in the painting's own lightness order (44 percent of its 57 within-painting matches) [3]. The earliest match dates to the year 1000, nearly a thousand years before the name's 1912 record, which shows only that a similar-looking hue existed in paint long before the word did, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. India is the most over-represented country, at 3.3 times its expected share, with Rajput paintings well above the archive's average [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [3].
